properties.title: A bad first night
properties.text: Nirvana's first Seattle gig, a Sub Pop Sunday booked by Jonathan Poneman. About twenty people came, the PA broke down, and Kurt Cobain said later: “We totally sucked.”
properties.why: Every scene story needs a bad first night. Seven months later Sub Pop put out Nirvana's first single, “Love Buzz”.

video.label: Nirvana back at the Vogue a year later, 21 June 1989: “Aero Zeppelin” (fan audio)

properties.title: The audition
properties.text: Nirvana opened a Sunday bill at the Pioneer Square tavern. Sub Pop's founders, Bruce Pavitt and Jonathan Poneman, came after hearing the band's demo.
properties.why: The show that led to Nirvana's deal with Sub Pop.

image.credit: Central Tavern in the 1970s. Seattle Municipal Archives, CC BY 2.0

properties.title: Sub Pop 200
properties.text: The release party for Sub Pop 200, a three-record box with Nirvana, Mudhoney, Soundgarden, TAD, Green River, Screaming Trees and more, wrapped in Charles Peterson's photographs.
properties.why: The label's statement of intent: a whole local scene packaged as one sound.
properties.note: Venue address from a single source.

video.label: Nirvana at the party, fan video

properties.title: Lame Fest ’89
properties.text: Sub Pop put three of its bands on one bill in a 1907 vaudeville theatre downtown. The sound was bad; Cobain dove into the drum kit.
properties.why: The scene moved out of the taverns and onto a real stage.

properties.title: The last Mother Love Bone show
properties.text: Mother Love Bone, the band the town expected to break first, played its final show at the Central. Singer Andrew Wood died of an overdose ten days later, before their debut album, Apple, came out.
properties.why: Wood's death split the band. Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament went on to form Pearl Jam, and Chris Cornell wrote the songs that became Temple of the Dog.

video.label: Mother Love Bone at the Central two months earlier, 6 January 1990 (fan audio, full show)

poster.credit: Central Tavern in the 1970s. Seattle Municipal Archives, CC BY 2.0

properties.title: Pearl Jam's first show
properties.text: Fifteen days after they first played together, Gossard, Ament, Mike McCready, Dave Krusen and a new singer from San Diego, Eddie Vedder, opened at the Off Ramp as Mookie Blaylock. About 300 people saw it.
properties.why: Chris Cornell called it “absolutely the best inaugural show I've seen in my life.” Ten months later Ten was out.

video.label: Full show, fan video (no single-song clip exists)

properties.title: A tribute, played once
properties.text: Chris Cornell's tribute to Andrew Wood, with Soundgarden's Matt Cameron and the band about to become Pearl Jam, played its only full show back at the Off Ramp.
properties.why: The album came out in April 1991 and only became a hit after Pearl Jam broke, with Cornell and Vedder trading lines on “Hunger Strike”.

properties.title: Live Facelift
properties.text: Alice in Chains filmed a hometown show for the home video Live Facelift. Mookie Blaylock opened and played “Why Go” and “Porch” for the first time; Cornell and Cameron joined them for “Hunger Strike” and “Say Hello 2 Heaven”.
properties.why: Two of the scene's biggest bands on one bill, before Pearl Jam even had its name.

video.label: Alice in Chains, “Man in the Box”

listen.label: Mookie Blaylock, “Alive”, same night, official audio

properties.bands: Nirvana, Fits of Depression, Bikini Kill
properties.title: A new song
properties.text: Nirvana introduced themselves as “major corporate rock sell-outs” and played a song with half-finished lyrics: “Smells Like Teen Spirit”.
properties.why: Its first performance anywhere. A few weeks later the band went to Los Angeles to record Nevermind.

poster.credit: The poster for the night. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

properties.title: The release party
properties.text: Bruce Pavitt DJed the Nevermind release party at a dance club on Howell Street. The band was thrown out after a food fight, and the state Liquor Control Board turned up.
properties.why: Nirvana's last night as a local band. Eleven days later Nevermind was in the shops.

properties.title: Halloween at the Paramount
properties.text: A Halloween homecoming with Mudhoney and Bikini Kill. The label filmed the whole show; some of the footage went into the “Lithium” video.
properties.why: Six months after the OK Hotel, Nevermind was out and the same band filled a 2,800-seat theatre.

listen.label: “Smells Like Teen Spirit” from the same night, official

properties.title: Motorvision
properties.text: Soundgarden, whose Screaming Life was among Sub Pop's first records, filmed the concert video Motorvision over two Paramount nights on the Badmotorfinger tour.
properties.why: The scene's elders, now on a major label, headlining downtown.

video.label: “Searching with My Good Eye Closed”, from Motorvision

properties.title: Drop in the Park
properties.text: Fresh off Lollapalooza with a gold record, Pearl Jam played a free, ticketed show for about 30,000 people at Magnuson Park. Around 3,000 registered to vote.
properties.why: Two years after 300 people at the Off Ramp.

video.label: Full show, remastered fan upload (single-song uploads are blocked from embedding)
video.short: Drop in the Park, full show

properties.title: Back in a club
properties.text: Nevermind had topped the Billboard chart in January. Nirvana opened for Mudhoney unannounced, skipped the hits, and played “Frances Farmer Will Have Her Revenge on Seattle” and “Very Ape” live for the first time.
properties.why: The biggest band in the world back in a Belltown club, playing the songs that would become In Utero.
